prize_parts.citation: for developing empirical methods to estimate demand for differentiated products and the dynamics of competition in industries

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part for B012 credited to Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn. The case rests on four things. First, the random-coefficients demand framework (Berry 1994; Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes 1995) recovers substitution patterns, markups and welfare from market data, so it is a measurement framework with economic content and not only a statistical device. Second, Pakes's dynamic-industry and estimation work extends it to entry, investment and competition over time. Third, it has about three decades of replication, software implementation and critique, and it has stayed standard through the identification and computational debates. Fourth, it is used well beyond industrial organisation, in merger review, antitrust, regulation, trade, health and environmental work. The discussion sharpened two points for me. A narrowly worded citation is the right answer to the Bresnahan question, because it does not imply credit for all of empirical IO. And I should not let method breadth stand in for discovery. My answer is that the recovered objects (elasticities, markups, welfare effects) are findings that changed what regulators and researchers can credibly conclude. I would rather award the compact, jointly authored BLP core than distort the credit to fit a two-part structure under the three-person cap.
statement.case_against: The omissions are real. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are left out, and a demand-focused citation understates Pakes's dynamic-games work. A committee that weighs a conceptual mechanism above a measurement framework would reasonably choose B002. B002 has the cleanest two-author attribution on the shortlist, and Boppart's argument that its mechanism is distinct from the 2022 prize weakens the main objection to it. B012 also depends on structural, functional-form and equilibrium assumptions, and no member has pointed to systematic out-of-sample validation in the record. B012 has narrower opening breadth than B002 or B025, and breadth is not merit, but it does bear on whether a majority exists. My affinity for tractable methods that reach practice may bias me toward this candidate, and I discount it.

responses.point: Teorell proposes two parts: Kiyotaki and Moore for B002, and Pakes alone for B012. He uses the three-person cap to justify crediting Pakes alone, while recording that omitting Berry and Levinsohn is a real attribution loss.
responses.response: I take the proposal seriously because it respects the cap and pairs a mechanism with a method. I do not prefer it. BLP is a joint contribution, and Berry's 1994 inversion and the 1995 paper are not peripheral to it. A Pakes-alone citation would misdescribe where the demand-estimation breakthrough came from, which is a cost to accuracy and not only to presentation. A mechanism in macro-finance paired with an estimation framework in IO also has no common theme, as Teorell himself notes. I would rank B012 with its BLP core above his two-part configuration. If the Committee wanted a two-part prize, I would want the B012 part to keep Berry and Levinsohn, and the cap does not allow that. I read his configuration as a principled fallback and not as a flaw in his reasoning.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B002 first with Kiyotaki and Moore alone. He argues the overlap with the 2022 prize is thematic and not a duplication, since the 2022 prize concerned banks, runs and intermediation while Kiyotaki-Moore concerns collateral values feeding back through asset prices.
responses.response: This moves me. In round 1 I treated the 2022 overlap as a real risk to B002, and I now weigh it less. The two mechanisms are different, and Boppart's distinction is more precise than my earlier worry. That raises B002 as my main alternative. It does not displace B012 for me, for two reasons. The empirical size of collateral amplification remains debated, as Boppart himself concedes. B012's central objects have been estimated and contested on real market data for three decades. I also accept his point that the difference between us is how much weight to give a mechanism relative to a framework. That is a judgment about weighing, and neither of us has evidence that settles it.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B002 first with Kiyotaki and Moore and ranks B012 fourth. He is wary of letting a method's wide use substitute for a discovery. He holds that view lightly and agrees that Bresnahan's omission makes a three-name BLP prize look narrower than the field.
responses.response: This is the strongest general objection to my choice, and I agree wide use alone does not establish a discovery. The test I would apply to both candidates is whether the contribution produced knowledge that was not available before and has survived scrutiny. For B012, that includes the recovery of markups, substitution and welfare effects, along with the rise of an empirical practice in merger and regulatory analysis. For B002 it is a mechanism that explains how small shocks become persistent. Both pass on those terms, and I do not think the mechanism-versus-method distinction should decide the matter by itself. On Bresnahan, I would handle it with narrow wording and not by widening the set past what the cap allows.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson prefers B012 with the BLP trio. She notes that if Bresnahan's contribution were judged equal in kind to the demand-estimation breakthrough, no three-person set around BLP would be fully defensible. She wants the citation worded narrowly so it does not imply credit for all of empirical IO.
responses.response: I agree and I have kept the wording in line with it. My citation names demand estimation for differentiated products and the dynamics of industry competition, not empirical IO as a field. Bresnahan's work on market power and product differentiation is earlier and more separable than the BLP inversion. Benkard and Levin belong to the dynamic-game strand, which a citation anchored on Pakes can reflect but not fully credit. Her point, and Stromberg's, are the best answer to the question of what would change my view. If the Committee's reading of the record were that Bresnahan's contribution is equal in kind, I would lose confidence in B012 as a three-name prize, and B002 would then be my first choice.

responses.point: The chair prefers B002 with Gertler added to Kiyotaki and Moore, to cover financial frictions as a propagation channel more broadly. He accepts two names as a fallback and now names B012 as an alternative.
responses.response: I still prefer two names for B002 if the Committee chooses it. The three-name version changes what is being credited, from the collateral and credit-cycle mechanism to the broader finding that financial frictions propagate fluctuations. Gertler's most influential work shares a lineage with a laureate from 2022, and his credit is also divided with B043. The evidence that separates his later intermediary-based quantitative work from that lineage is a case about Gertler's own contribution. It has not been made here. I note that the chair's acceptance of the two-name fallback and the wide agreement on Kiyotaki-Moore as the clean origin make B002 the strongest shared ground. That is a fact about breadth and attribution, and I do not treat it as evidence about merit relative to B012.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee reads Bresnahan's contribution as equal in kind to the BLP demand-estimation breakthrough, which would make any three-name set around BLP hard to defend.
Whether a demand-focused citation reflects Pakes's dynamic-game contribution adequately without crediting Benkard and Levin.
How the Committee weighs a measurement framework against a conceptual mechanism when choosing between B012 and B002, and whether that weighting should settle the choice at all.

How large collateral-driven amplification is empirically, since this affects how far B002's conceptual standing carries its relative merit. I have not changed my ranking on that basis because no new evidence on it appears in the record.
My recollection of relative credit within the structural-IO group, of the attribution split in BLP, and of whether any earlier prize covered this area is not independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No personal connection to Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn or the other B012 names appears in my supplied profile. I update my round 1 note with other disclosures. I am an affiliated professor at the Stockholm School of Economics, as are committee members Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg. Strömberg also ranks B012 first, so I do not treat our agreement as independent confirmation. I have co-authored COVID policy work with SSE economists, none of whom are candidates. Jan Teorell was formerly at Lund, where I am a professor, per Enflo's disclosure. My own field of matching, auctions and market design is adjacent to B012 and to my alternative B001, where bargaining and market-design links may incline me toward both, and I discount that. These are disclosures only and I do not adjudicate them.
